en: When both the Senate and House of Representatives pass a bill and the President signs it, it becomes law.
When the Katipuneros publicly tore their tax certificates, they rejected Spanish authority, sparking the official start of the Philippine Revolution.
Mountain springs feed the Ifugao rice terraces, causing water to flow downward through interconnected stone channels to irrigate every descending paddy.
Farmers boil and dye leaf sheaths, then stack them to form kiping, creating edible decorations for the annual Pahiyas Festival.
T'boli women extract abaca fibers, dye them with natural plant colors, and weave them into T'nalak cloth inspired by dream visions.
Citizens who reach eighteen years of age and register with the election commission automatically gain the right to vote in national elections.
Farmers guide the carabao with a halter, utilizing its massive physical strength to plow muddy fields and prepare soil for planting rice.
Dr. Fe del Mundo designed a bamboo incubator where hot water jars radiate heat to keep premature babies warm without electricity.
Artisans carve specific dots and lines onto bamboo using a stylus, where each Baybayin symbol produces a distinct spoken syllable.
Voters elect a Punong Barangay and councilors, who then convene to pass local ordinances and resolve everyday neighborhood disputes.
Jose Rizal wrote Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo, exposing Spanish friar abuses that awakened Filipino nationalism and inspired the revolution.
A Kalinga mambabatok taps soot mixed with water into the skin using a citrus thorn, creating permanent traditional body patterns.
